title: Freedom of Expression
byline: compiled and edited by Sita Ram Goel · Voice of India · late 1990s · subtitled Secular Theocracy Versus Liberal Democracy
lede: This is a dossier rather than an argued book. It collects the court orders in five criminal cases against Hindu writers and speakers, the press record of Goel's own 1987 arrest, essays by Arun Shourie, Ram Swarup and Koenraad Elst on book bans, and thirteen reviews of Ibn Warraq's Why I Am Not a Muslim. Goel's long preface argues that Indian “secularism” has become a theocracy that shields one religion from criticism.
facts: criminal cases under sections 153-A and 295-A of the Indian Penal Code, each ending in discharge
the longest wait: Goel's own case, from 1986 to 1997
when “secular” was written into the Constitution's Preamble, during the Emergency, as Goel notes
reviews of Ibn Warraq's 1995 book, mostly by Western rationalists
note: Most of this book reprints court orders and other people's essays. The reviews in the last third are strongly hostile to Islam. This page summarises what the documents record and what the contributors argue, attributed to them, and does not endorse their views.

sections.title: Five prosecutions, five discharges
sections.lede: Each case was brought under laws against promoting enmity between groups (153-A) or outraging religious feelings (295-A). In every one the magistrate found no prima facie case. The bars show the years from the case being registered to discharge.
items: FIR 1983, discharged 31 July 1986. He published Quran verses from a Hindi translation by a Muslim scholar. The court found no malice in quoting the verses as they stood.
FIR 1986 for publishing Colin Maine's The Dead Hand of Islam. Discharged 17 May 1997: the charge was “groundless”.
Two cases (1986, 1988) over two newspaper articles. Discharged 5 May 1990: one was narrated history, the other opinion, neither malicious.
FIR 1991 over a speech. Discharged 2 July 1996: no recording or transcript connected him to it.
Speech of 29 November 1990, FIR 1991. Discharged 13 February 1996: the case “appears to be influenced by political forces”.
sections.note: Years run from the year the case was registered to the year of discharge, as given in the orders reprinted in the book. For Bali, the later of the two cases is used.

sections.title: Understanding Islam through Hadis
sections.lede: Ram Swarup's study of the Hadith was not banned in English for nine years. Goel's account of what happened once a Hindi translation was printed.
items: By Voice of India, without objection.
Police seize 2,000 copies at the binder and arrest Goel.
A statement signed by Dharampal, Nirmal Verma and others; reported in the Indian Express and the Times of India.
The Delhi Administration, having screened the book twice, recommends closure.
By notification of the same Administration.
After eight years in circulation in India.

sections.eyebrow: Chapters 10–15 · bans and the people behind them
sections.title: A short chain of bans
items: Banned in India. Elst names Syed Shahabuddin as instrumental.
Pro-Vice-Chancellor Mushirul Hasan says the ban should go, and retracts under student protest.
Hindi edition, then the English original.
Shahabuddin asks the Home Ministry to ban Ram Swarup's 1992 book. Intellectuals sign a statement against it.

sections.title: What the magistrates looked for
sections.lede: The orders cite a run of precedents, from Allahabad (1927) to the Supreme Court (1957). Read together they set a recognisable test.

items: Deliberate, malicious intent to outrage a community
Speech shown by evidence to have caused enmity

sections.title: “Secular theocracy”
items: Goel notes that “secularism” is absent from Nehru's pre-1947 vocabulary and from the 1950 Constitution.
Indira Gandhi inserted it into the Preamble in 1976.
Missionaries and mullahs, whose own doctrines prescribe theocracy, now defend Indian secularism, as Communists once defended democracy.
He argues the laws on hurt sentiments are used to put Islam beyond questioning, while criticism of Hinduism goes unpunished.

sections.title: Thirteen reviewers of Why I Am Not a Muslim (1995)
sections.lede: Reprinted to show, in Goel's framing, that what Indian courts are asked to ban is mainstream scholarship abroad. The reviewers range from rationalist philosophers to ex-Muslims.
